matrix.protected_work: Preserve the necessary-and-sufficient existence argument, sign boundary and uniqueness warrant; hints may clarify quantifiers and domain but may not conclude which k works.

task.title: Prove an exponential-equation existence criterion
task.stem: Let a>1 and k be real. Prove exactly for which k the equation a^(2x+1)=(a^2)^x+k has a real solution, and prove uniqueness when it exists. Address the boundary k=0. Then explain how the criterion changes if 0<a<1.
task.expected_attempt: State and justify necessity, sufficiency and uniqueness; verify edge cases and changed-base assumption. Numerical trials alone do not establish the universal claim.
task.misconception: Uses one example as proof, ignores strict positivity, or extends a>1 sign conclusion to bases between 0 and 1.

difficulty.basis: Author evidence: a universal iff proof needs a valid substitution, positivity sign condition, surjective/injective exponential reasoning, and an exception for 0<a<1; derived D4.

grade9v3:cognitive_demand.basis: The decisive work is establishing a universally valid necessary-and-sufficient warrant including uniqueness and domain exception.

grade9v3:analysis.stable_crux_move: Prove necessity, sufficiency and uniqueness under the stated base domain; distinguish the reversed-sign exception.
grade9v3:analysis.common_wrong_route: Treat a successful numeric trial or a guessed k sign as proof for all real x and all positive bases.

reasoning_route.action: Establish the sign-compatible necessary-and-sufficient condition and unique inverse exponent from t=a^(2x)>0, and re-evaluate the sign when 0<a<1.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Positive-base real exponentials range over (0,infinity) and are injective for a>0, a!=1; the coefficient (a-1) has a fixed sign.
reasoning_route.output: A complete iff argument, uniqueness and base-domain exception, not an example.

rungs.text: Separate what is given about a, k and x from what you must establish: existence, nonexistence and uniqueness.
Which properties of positive-base real exponentials are relevant to their values and to whether two exponents can give the same value?
Organize the argument into necessity, sufficiency and uniqueness. Check the boundary cases and the changed base interval; you must choose the decisive inference yourself.

core1a_repair.trigger: Learner takes one numerical instance as proof, overlooks range/positivity, or falsely carries a sign condition across different base domains.

sequence.text: Away from a and k, consider Z=2^r for real r. Can Z be zero or negative? Check how Z behaves for very large positive and negative r.

For a positive base b other than 1, b^r ranges over all positive numbers, and equal output values require equal exponents. Explain why existence needs a permissible output and uniqueness needs one-to-one behaviour.
Let Z=4^q>0. Could either Z=-2 or Z=0 be attained? Could two different real q give Z=16? Explain all three claims, without referring to a or k.
On an unrelated relation with a known sign, compare the possibility of 3Z=12 and -2Z=12 under Z>0. Distinguish one example from a proof of a universal criterion.
For a different base b=1/2, determine with proof which real m permit (1/2)^(2y+1)=(1/4)^y+m, including uniqueness and zero as a boundary.

reviewer_only.expected_explanation: Let t=a^(2x)>0. The equation becomes (a-1)t=k. For a>1, a-1>0, so a positive t exists iff k>0; then t=k/(a-1)>0 and a^(2x)=t has exactly one real solution x=(log_a t)/2. k=0 and k<0 are impossible. For 0<a<1, a-1<0, so existence and uniqueness instead require k<0. The excluded a=1 case is degenerate and not part of either interval.
reviewer_only.concept_check: 4^q>0 always, so neither zero nor -2 occurs. Base 4 exponentiation is one-to-one; only q=2 gives 16.
reviewer_only.fresh_exit: For b=1/2, the coefficient b-1=-1/2, and t=b^(2y)>0 requires m<0. Then t=-2m>0, giving one real y via log_b(t)/2; m=0 or m>0 gives no real y.
